rationale: This empirical health/development economics paper investigates the Hindu-Muslim infant mortality puzzle in India, showing that neighborhood sanitation externalities explain why children in Muslim neighborhoods have higher survival to age one. It does not examine any legal, administrative, regulatory, tenure, tariff, or institutional mechanism governing sanitation service access (failing Criterion 2 under both narrow and plain readings, E03), and its primary outcome is infant mortality rather than water/sanitation service access (failing Criterion 4).
plain_vs_narrow_note: No divergence between plain and narrow Criterion 2 readings: the study examines religious neighborhood composition and sanitation health externalities on infant mortality rather than any legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance mechanism.

evidence_quotes.quote: externalities due to poor sanitation are a channel linking the religious composition of neighborhoods to infant mortality.
Muslim children are substantially more likely than Hindu children to survive to their first birthday
